Apple has been fighting to continue taking a commission on app sales made through third-party stores, and its hardline stance has angered the judge in its long-running lawsuit with Epic Games.

The company subsequently submitted a more moderate proposal, offering to reduce commission rates, but acknowledged in new regulatory filings that it could ultimately end up collecting no commission at all on such sales…

Apple's App Commission Battle

Antitrust regulators around the world have taken issue with the fact that developers have historically only been able to sell iPhone apps and in-app content through Apple's official App Store. This monopoly has allowed the Cupertino company to set its own commission rates, leaving iPhone developers with no choice but to accept them.

The European Union was the first region to force Apple to open up third-party app stores, while a US court has ruled that Apple must allow developers to offer in-app purchases and subscriptions through external payment platforms.

Apple significantly angered the judge in the US case by charging a 27% commission on in-app content sales, even when the transaction was not conducted through the App Store. After deducting roughly 3% in payment processing fees, this means the commission Apple collects is exactly the same regardless of whether developers sell through the Apple Store or not.

The judge pointed out that this is clearly an abuse of the spirit of the ruling, while Apple argues that the court has not prescribed an acceptable commission rate for external sales.

Lower Commission Rates

Apple has recently filed a more restrained commission proposal for sales conducted outside the App Store.

  • Standard apps at 15%, compared with the current 30% in-app purchase (IAP) commission rate for such apps;
  • Video Partner Program (VPP), News Partner Program (NPP), Mini Apps Partner Program (MPP), and subscription renewals at 10%;
  • Apps under the Small Business Program at 5%.

The company hopes the court will view these compromise rates as fair and reasonable, reflecting the cost of providing developers with Xcode and other tools to help create apps.

But Admitted It May End Up With Nothing

However, while Apple is hoping to be permitted to charge these lower commissions, it acknowledged in a new regulatory filing that it may ultimately be unable to collect any commission on purchases made through third-party app stores and other external platforms. The Financial Times reports:

Analysts note that services revenue could therefore decline for the first time, affecting the company's valuation.
